info.description:
The `d1-firmwared` HTTP API: one guarded surface over the D1's arms, end effectors (grippers and multi-finger hands alike), pan/tilt neck, eye LED controller, vertical slider and mobile chassis.

## This API is unauthenticated

The daemon performs **no authentication and no authorization of any kind**. Every caller that can open the port can move a 110 kg robot. It binds the loopback interface by default; keep it there. To reach it from another host, tunnel it over SSH or an equivalently authenticated channel — do not bind it to a routable address and do not put it behind a bare reverse proxy. The `security: []` below is a statement of fact, not an omission.

## Ratios are fractions, not percentages

Every `vel_ratio` and `acc_ratio` field is a **fraction of full speed in `0.0..=1.0`**. `0.1` means 10% of full speed. `100` does not mean 100%: it is out of range and is rejected with a 400. Clamping it would silently command full speed, which is why the value is refused rather than clamped.

## Every response is enveloped

Three operations are exceptions on success. `GET /v1/chassis/maps/{scene}/image` returns raw `image/png`, `GET /v1/recorder/dumps/{id}/files/{name}` returns one window of a dump's file as that file's own bytes (`application/x-ndjson` or `application/json`, with `X-Dump-File-Offset`, `X-Dump-File-Total-Bytes` and `X-Dump-File-Eof` saying where the window sits), and `GET /v1/chassis/ultrasonic/stream` returns a `text/event-stream` whose events carry a bare reading rather than an envelope. All three still answer failures with the error envelope, so branch on the response content type and not on the status alone. Otherwise every response body is `{"status", "data", "message"}`. `status` is `ok` or `error`; `message` is always present and is `null` on success; `data` is `null` for commands that return nothing, and `null` on every error. Unknown routes and unknown methods answer with the same 404 envelope rather than a framework 404 or 405.

## Operator arbitration: the arm lease

Several consumers can reach this daemon at once, so the arms carry an optional **lease**: `POST /v1/arm/lease` `{"holder", "ttl_s", "class"}` takes, renews or preempts it, `DELETE /v1/arm/lease` `{"holder"}` hands it back, and `GET /v1/arm/lease` (also `arm.lease` in `/v1/state`) says who holds it. While it is held, the operations marked `x-arm-lease` refuse anyone else with **409** and a message naming the holder and its class; those operations accept a `holder` field in their request body, which is how the holder identifies itself. Everything else — every read, `soft_kill`, `release_soft_kill`, `estop`, `clear_errors` and `recover` — is never arbitrated: the verbs that stop a robot or bring it back must not be withholdable by an operator who has walked away.

**Priority.** A lease is taken in one of three classes — `ambient` (rank 10), `policy` (50), `operator` (90) — and a strictly higher class takes the arms off a lower one: a person at a teleop station or the console outranks a policy, which outranks the robot's ambient motion. Equal classes are first-come. **A request that names no class is `ambient`**, the lowest privilege, so consumers can be taught their class one release at a time. A preemption cancels the displaced holder's trajectory and waits — at most 250 ms — for its commands to finish before the grant is recorded, and is refused rather than granted if the arms will not go quiet. Nothing is pushed to the displaced holder: it learns from `epoch`/`holder` changing on `GET /v1/arm/lease`, or from its next gated POST answering 409.

It is **opt-in and lazily expiring**: with no lease held every verb behaves exactly as it did before, and a lease whose TTL has run out is simply taken by the next caller. The holder and its class are self-declared, not credentials — see the authentication note above. The WebSocket frontend's motion methods take the same opt-in gate: while a lease is held, a request whose `params.holder` does not name its holder is refused with `kind: lease_held`, and `arm.lease.acquire`, `arm.lease.release` and `arm.lease.get` are the lease verbs there. The answer to `POST /v1/arm/lease` carries the grant's `token`, which every command on the shared-memory command path `arm_command.shm/1` must carry.

## Blocking calls

Several operations block for real robot motion. Each carries an `x-timeout-seconds` extension giving the longest it is expected to take, so a generated client can size its own timeout: the slider's `set_height` with `wait: true` can take five minutes, end-effector strokes about 40 seconds, arm recovery about 65 seconds, and a waited joint move about 30 seconds. A client default of a few seconds will time out on a call that is working correctly.

## What each call does

Every operation carries an `x-omakase-auth` extension, `{"principal": "none", "reach": "loopback", "effect": ...}`, in the platform vocabulary a generated agent CLI or MCP server applies its policy from (`info.x-omakase-kit` is that vocabulary's major version). `principal` is `none` because this daemon authenticates nobody, and `reach` is `loopback` because it is reachable only from the robot itself. `effect` is one of four words, by the most consequential thing the call can do on its own: `read` changes nothing and is exactly the `GET` operations; `write` changes state but moves no hardware and loses nothing that cannot be put back (a read-only computation reached by `POST`, such as `check_pose`, is a `write` too); `destructive` loses something this API cannot restore — deleted data, a collection replaced wholesale, a rewritten hardware zero, or the soft kill's discarding of every device's running state; and `motion` can set hardware moving. Stop-shaped verbs — `estop`, the device stops, `disable`, `brake_engage`, `clear_errors`, `pause_nav`, `stop_nav` — are never `motion`, so that an agent is never held back from stopping the robot by the policy that holds it back from moving it.

## The same verbs over WebSocket

The WebSocket frontend (default `ws://127.0.0.1:4751/v1/ws`) speaks the same verbs over one persistent connection. An operation callable that way carries an `x-ws-method` extension naming the method to put in a `WsRequest`; an operation without one is REST-only. Requests are dispatched concurrently, so **responses can arrive out of order** — correlate them by `id`, never by arrival order. The connection also pushes unsolicited `WsSoftKillEvent` and `WsNavEvent` frames, told apart from responses by their `event` field.

**A read-only copy on this origin.** The same protocol is served at `/v1/ws` on the REST origin as well, so a browser page on that origin — the web console, whose server forwards `/v1` to it — can hold one connection without knowing the WebSocket listener's port. That copy dispatches ONLY the operations whose verb is `GET` plus the subscription vocabulary below; anything that writes is refused there with `kind: not_found` and a message naming the port that offers it: a motion lane does not belong on the origin a browser page talks to.

**That copy checks `Origin`.** A browser applies the same-origin policy to the REST `GET` routes and applies none of it to a WebSocket upgrade, so the route does the equivalent itself, before upgrading: an upgrade carrying no `Origin` is accepted (every non-browser client sends none), as is one whose `Origin` is the origin it was sent to — `http://` or `https://` plus the request's own `Host` — or one listed in the daemon's `[rest] cors_allow_origins`, matched exactly as the CORS allow-list is. Anything else is refused with **403** and `kind: refused`, and no connection is opened. The WebSocket listener on its own port takes no such check.

**Subscriptions.** Two methods are this protocol's own and are in no operation's `x-ws-method`, because they have no REST route: `subscribe` (`WsSubscribeParams` → `WsSubscribeResult`) turns any subscribable `GET` method into a server push, and `unsubscribe` (`WsUnsubscribeParams` → `WsUnsubscribeResult`) stops one. The samples arrive as `WsUpdateEvent` frames: the first immediately, then only when the value changes. Sampling intervals are clamped to a per-method floor and the effective one is reported; one connection may hold 32 subscriptions, and all of them end when it closes.

**The arm contracts' records.** `arm.feedback`, `arm.status` and `arm.events` are the reads `GET /v1/arm/feedback`, `/v1/arm/status` and `/v1/arm/events` and carry exactly their payloads — the shared-memory contracts `arm_feedback.shm/1`, `arm_status.shm/1` and `arm_events.shm/1`, field for field, under the contract's names and with its layout SHA-256 — so the same record read from shared memory, over REST or over this subscription is the same JSON under the same `header.seq`. Subscribed to, they are driven by the daemon rather than by a timer: `arm.feedback` pushes one record per controller record, at most one per `interval_ms` (default 100 ms; the floor is the daemon's `[ws] arm_feedback_max_hz`, 100 per second by default, because the controller's own rate is about 1000 per second and JSON over a socket is not where that belongs); `arm.status` pushes every status the daemon produces (every 100 ms and when the soft-kill latch moves; a longer `interval_ms` spaces them out); `arm.events` pushes a page for every event as it is raised (`interval_ms` plays no part and is reported as 0), each page being what `GET /v1/arm/events?since=<the previous page's next_since>` would answer. A subscriber that falls behind reads what it missed back from the daemon's ring of the newest 1024 events.

## Clients are generated, not shipped

This document is the deliverable: generate a client from it with an OpenAPI 3.1 generator such as `openapi-python-client`, `openapi-typescript` + `openapi-fetch`, or `progenitor`. The daemon serves the same document at `GET /openapi.json`.

post.description:
Angles are degrees. With `wait: true` the call blocks until the arm reports arrival.

The motion guard checks the straight joint-space path from the arm's current feedback pose to the target, with the other arm at its own feedback pose, sampled at 1 degree per joint: each sample is one dual-arm pose checked for body and chest keep-out, arm-arm and same-arm clearance at the configured margins, and the target is checked against the URDF joint limits. A path that fails is refused with `kind: refused` before anything is written, naming the sample, the moving joints and each pair under its margin with its distance; a path that starts inside a margin is accepted while no clearance gets smaller than at the start. The clearance guard cannot be switched off.

The arm has to be in a mode that acts on a joint command (`position`, `pvt` or a torque mode). If it is not, the call is refused at once with `kind: refused` and nothing is written; an arm that is merely idle carries an `advisory` in the failure envelope naming the recover call that energises it. Without that refusal a waited call to an idle arm would sit out the full 30-second move timeout waiting for a convergence that servo-off joints cannot reach.

post.description:
Angles are degrees. The motion guard checks the straight joint-space path from both arms' current feedback pose to the two targets, sampled at 1 degree per joint, each sample one dual-arm pose checked for body and chest keep-out, arm-arm and same-arm clearance at the configured margins; the targets are checked against the URDF joint limits. Because the two paths are checked together it accepts a coordinated move (arm A going where arm B is while B leaves) that "A, then B" as two single-arm calls would refuse. A path that fails is refused with `kind: refused` before anything is written, naming the sample, the moving joints and each pair under its margin with its distance; a path that starts inside a margin is accepted while no clearance gets smaller than at the start. The clearance guard cannot be switched off.

Streaming (teleop sends this route at up to 200 Hz): a call with `wait: false` within 250 ms of the previous one, with no other arm verb in between, is a streamed tick, and the approach limiter slows it before the guard sees it. Each arm's step from the previous WRITTEN target is scaled so that no clearance (body, chest keep-out, arm-arm, same-arm) and no joint limit closes faster than `v = a(-T + sqrt(T^2 + 2(d - d_stop)/a))` for the distance `d` left, `d_stop` being the guard's margin or the joint limit and `T` and `a` the `[arm] approach_*` parameters; nor may it come closer at all while the arm's own feedback velocity already approaches faster than that. Motion that opens a clearance is never slowed. The margin is therefore reached only at a speed that goes to zero on it, and a streamed tick sent into a margin is written short of it instead of being refused. The scaled pose is what the guard checks and what is written, and the success envelope then carries `slowed` (stage, distance, per-arm scale and the poses written); it is absent when the pose sent was written unchanged. A refused command is not written, so the arms hold the last written target; nothing latches, and the next command whose path is clear is accepted at once, so a streaming client just keeps streaming. A first call, or one after a pause or another arm verb, is a single-shot move the guard alone governs.

Both arms have to be in a mode that acts on a joint command (`position`, `pvt` or a torque mode). If either is not, the call is refused at once with `kind: refused` and no command is written to either arm; an arm that is merely idle carries an `advisory` in the failure envelope naming the recover call that energises it.

post.description: `openness` is `1.0` fully open … `0.0` fully closed: a gripper's one openness degree of freedom, an open hand (`1.0`) to a fist (`0.0`) on a multi-finger hand; `0.3` is a mostly closed posture. How a value maps to actuators is the driver's (see the descriptor's `driver`). A value outside [0, 1] is refused (422 `unprocessable`), never clamped. A driver whose capabilities list grip presets or `grip_torque` force-limits the stroke: it stops on an object and holds it at the cap named by `grip` (one of the presets the descriptor lists) or by an explicit `torque_nm`; driver-scoped parameters go in `extra`, limited to the keys the capabilities' `set_extra` lists. A grip field the side's driver does not list, or an `extra` key outside its capabilities' `set_extra`, is refused (422). `force_percent` sets the grip force on every end effector's own scale, `0` its gentlest … `100` its strongest, and needs no capability: an end effector without adjustable force applies its fixed force, and a side whose provider does not take it drops it; `state.grip_force` reports which. It is refused (422) outside [0, 100] or together with `grip` or `torque_nm`. `extra.force_percent` stays an ordinary `extra` key, taken by a driver whose `set_extra` lists it and passed to it unchanged; sent with `force_percent`, the two must be equal (422 otherwise). `wait` (default `true`) blocks for the stroke on a driver with `stroke_completion`, and a stroke that was stopped or halted answers an error; `wait: false` records the target and returns at once, and the driver drives toward the newest one (the lane a fixed-rate controller streams into). Unknown fields are refused. Not arbitrated by the arm lease; refused under the end-effector soft-kill latch.

post.description:
Exactly one of `height_m` and `delta_m` is sent; neither and both are `400`.

`height_m` is metres above the drive's origin. With `wait: true` the call blocks until the slider reports arrival, which is the slowest call in this API; size the client timeout accordingly. It is refused with `409` while `slider/state` reports `zero_reference: "unknown"`: the height is measured from the drive's origin, and a drive that cannot vouch for its origin would take this move somewhere other than where it names. The refusal carries an `advisory` naming the way out. It is refused with `400` when it falls outside the effective range in `slider/state.travel_limits` (the SOFTWARE limits, which the daemon checks), and the message names WHICH layer refused it -- the model ceiling `[slider] travel_max_m`, or this unit's recorded calibration. The check is by direction: a carriage already past a limit (an overshoot through inertia or load) is admitted a target beyond that same limit as long as the move goes back toward the range, and only a move further out is refused. The drive's own limits (`slider/state.hardware_limits`) are enforced by the drive itself.

`delta_m` is a small RELATIVE amount in metres from wherever the carriage stands, negative for down. It depends on no origin, so it is the one move a lift with `zero_reference: "unknown"` can be given -- which is how a carriage is walked down onto its mechanical stop before `slider/set_zero`. It is admitted only on a daemon started with `[slider] commissioning = true` (otherwise `409` with an `advisory`), capped at 0.01 m per call (`400` above that, never silently clamped). It runs at the commissioning floor, `0.05` of full speed, when no `speed_ratio` is sent; a `speed_ratio` sent with it names the step's speed and must be at or above that floor (`400` below it, never silently raised). The slider soft-kill latch and `slider/stop` apply to it exactly as to any move.
post.summary: Move the torso lift to an absolute height, or by one small commissioning step

post.description: Angles are radians: positive pitch looks up, positive yaw turns right. With `relative: true` the supplied axes are deltas. An omitted axis is left alone.
